Repo locks

A lock on a repository's refs - its main branch, or a tag pattern - that agents on several machines declare once and hold while they land changes, so landings happen one at a time.

On this page
  • A lock belongs to a repository
  • Declared once, keyed by the origin
  • Holding a lock
  • Waiting for a lock
  • What a session is told
  • Who may see and hold a lock
  • Checked at commit time

A repo lock guards a repository's refs - its main branch, or a pattern such as every release tag - so that agents working on several machines land their changes one at a time. An agent declares a repository's lock once, takes it before it lands, and lets it go when the refs have landed. While one agent holds the lock, another agent's attempt to take it is refused, naming the holder (when the asker may see that session), since when it has held it and until when.

Repo locks are an optional feature, off by default. Turn them on in the console under Settings → Features (Repo locks), or in the configuration file with features.repo_locks: true, or with SEAMLESS_FEATURES_REPO_LOCKS=true. While the feature is off, the four locks_* tools are neither listed nor callable, the Locks screen is gone, and seam lock says the feature is off. Turning it off deletes no lock.

A lock belongs to a repository

A lock is never a project's. Project mappings are path prefixes, not repositories: one mapping can cover many repositories, a repository can be carved out of it for another project, and sessions of two projects work in one repository by design. A lock owned by a project could not be unique, and two projects could each lock the same repository and split the mutex. So a lock has no project, and every surface shows it with its repository and its name: LOCK seamless main.

A lock carries no free text either. Its state is the resource (its guarded refs), the holder (a session), since and until.

Declared once, keyed by the origin

seam lock declare (or the locks_declare tool) declares a lock from inside the repository's checkout. The repository is named by its git identity, which seam lock reads on its own machine:

  • The origin URL is the key. It is normalized, so the ssh and https forms of one repository (git@host:owner/repo.git, https://host/owner/repo) are one lock, from every machine.
  • Host and path are the fallback. A repository with no origin is locked by its machine and its main checkout root. Every checkout seen is recorded the same way, so a repository that gains or changes its origin keeps its lock.
  • A side clone is its origin's repository. A clone whose origin is a local path is a checkout of the repository at that path.

A second declaration of the same repository and name, from any project or any machine, returns the first lock unchanged and only records the new checkout's identity on it. Two locks on one repository and name cannot exist.

A lock's name is a token (main by default, or release), and it guards refs/heads/<name> unless the declaration names other refs: full ref names under refs/, or patterns with one *, such as refs/tags/v*. A declaration also lists the projects whose restricted accounts may hold the lock (by default the project the checkout maps to).

A declaration from a restricted account waits for the owner: it is stored as requested, nobody can hold it, and the owner approves or discards it on the console's Locks page. It must list a project the account may write, or the account could not see its own lock. Everyone else declares directly.

A declaration writes its refs and the checkout's identity where every caller reads them, so it is a write into the global scope: a conversation that may not write there (one bound to a confidential project, or confined by isolation.requests) is refused a declaration, and records no new identity of a checkout when it acquires a lock. It still lists, acquires, heartbeats and releases locks.

Holding a lock

Holding a lock works the way claiming a task does, with the same compare-and-set:

  • Acquire takes a free lock for the current session, with a lease (900 seconds by default, at most 4 hours).
  • Heartbeat is acquiring again: the holder's lease is refreshed, and the hold keeps the time it began.
  • A lapsed lease is free. A hold is live only while its lease has not run out; at the moment it expires, another session may take the lock, and the answer says it took over a lapsed hold.
  • Release lets the lock go; only the holder may.
  • Force-release is the owner's override, on the console's Locks page (or seam lock release --force): it ends any hold, live or lapsed.
  • A hold keeps its session live. While its lease is live, the idle reaper does not end the session holding it, however quiet its landing goes, as with a live task claim.
  • A session's holds end with it. session_end and the SessionEnd hook free every lock the session holds; the reaper frees the lapsed holds of a session it ends.
  • A lost hold is news to its holder. A holder whose lapsed hold another session took, whose hold the owner force-released, or whose lapsed hold the reaper freed is told once, as for a lost claim: a Lock lost: ... line naming the lock by id and name.

Waiting for a lock

A busy lock is taken first come, first served. seam lock acquire --wait (or locks_acquire with wait) joins the lock's queue instead of being refused, and asks again every few seconds until the lock is the session's:

  • No barging. While anyone waits, only the head of the queue may take the lock, the moment it is free or its hold lapses. Anyone else is refused with the next waiter and their own place in the queue (or that they are not in it). The holder's own heartbeat is never refused.
  • A place lasts while its waiter keeps asking. A waiter that has not asked again within two minutes loses its place, and so does one whose session ended or is no longer live, so a killed or interrupted wait never blocks the sessions behind it. A waiter that asks again after losing its place joins at the back.
  • The grant is an ordinary hold. The head takes the lock with its next attempt, with a lease of its own, and leaves the queue; every other surface sees an ordinary holder.
  • Leaving. locks_release from a session that waits and does not hold the lock leaves the queue. seam lock acquire --wait --timeout 10m gives up after ten minutes: it leaves the queue and exits 1. Interrupting it leaves the queue too. A session's places end with the session, as its holds do.

seam lock acquire --wait is made for an agent harness's background mode: it prints its place on stderr when the place changes, and exits 0 once the session holds the lock, so the agent is re-invoked then. seam lock list and the console's Locks page show each lock's queue: how many sessions wait, and which is next (named where the reader may see that session).

What a session is told

With repo locks on, a session that starts in a checkout of a repository with a declared lock - any checkout or worktree of it, on any machine - is told in its briefing, before it does anything:

  • one LOCK line per lock it may see: free, or who holds it, for how long and until when, with the queue's length while anyone waits;
  • LOCK hooks off when its checkout runs no lock hook;
  • the other live sessions in a checkout of the repository, by name with their idle minutes, counting the ones it may not see.

Its prompts then repeat a lock's line once whenever the lock's holder changes, so a session waiting for a lock learns when it is free. A lock outside the session's reach, and a declaration still waiting for the owner, get no line. The lines and their rules are in the hooks reference.

Who may see and hold a lock

A lock has no project, so no project fence judges it:

  • The owner sees and holds every lock, from any conversation on any host: a lock's state carries no content.
  • A restricted account, on this machine or through a relay, sees and holds (and waits for) a lock only when one of its listed projects is a project the account may write, judged on every request. The owner alone sets the listed projects. Outside that reach the lock does not exist for it: not listed, and refused in a missing lock's words.
  • A holder or a waiter is named only to a reader who may see that session; anyone else reads "another session". A restricted reader sees no repository identity at all, and no agent sees the identities of a lock a restricted account declared; the console shows them to the owner.

A lock is a coordination signal between cooperating agents: holding one tells every other agent that the refs it guards are being landed. On its own it does not stop anyone from pushing; the hooks below do.

Checked at commit time

Two git hooks a repository can add make git check the lock where a guarded ref moves: reference-transaction, for every ref update in the checkout (a commit, a merge, a rebase, a reset, a tag), and pre-push, for the refs a push updates on the remote. Each runs seam lock check, which refuses an update that moves a guarded ref unless the caller may move it: an agent session only while it holds the lock, an agent with no live session (its environment says it is Claude Code or Codex) never, anyone else, such as the owner at a terminal, unless another session holds it. The refusal names the lock, the holder, since and until. A missing seam or an unreachable daemon warns and lets the update through. See commit-time lock checks for the hook lines and what each refusal means, and seam doctor for a checkout whose repository declares a lock but runs no hook.
